rule_name: an absence verdict names the search space it exhausted
pattern: A step refuses a thing the distribution DOES declare, in a view the step never opened, and the refusal reads as thorough because it carries a count over the one view it did open. Every part of the count is measured and true. A reader cannot tell 'I looked in the two places this is declared and it is in neither' from 'I looked in one of them', because both print the same sentence and only one of them is a finding about the input. The defect survives review precisely because the disclosure looks complete: a denominator is present, so the usual question -- did this examine anything? -- has already been answered yes.
docstring: Every absence-class refusal must carry an ADDRESS: something that tells the reader where the program looked. The repo already asks a PASS to disclose how much it examined; this asks the same question of a REFUSAL, which is the half that was open. An address is a filesystem path, a glob, an environment reference, or a document pointer -- an address is an address whether or not it has a slash in it. What the rule cannot decide from source alone is whether the address is COMPLETE, because completeness is a property of the distribution and not of our code; that half needs the artefact to record which view each resolved value came from, and it is named as out of reach rather than pretended away.
fix_action: Parse every module under the programs tree and collect each refusal CONSTRUCTION whose rule id matches the repo's own absence convention. Require an address among the refusal's companions, resolving one level of local binding (a reason built from the path one line above) and one level of enclosing call (a refusal nested inside the report that carries the paths). Exclude lookups, which are not refusals, and exclude test fixtures, which are deliberately minimal. Report file, line and rule id for each refusal that names nowhere. Answer NOT CHECKED, never PASS, when the directory is absent or the population is empty. MEASURED: the predicate was narrowed four times, each narrowing removing a real false positive rather than a hypothetical one; the surviving population is 31 absence verdicts over 1277 files, and the two genuine findings were fixed by ADDING information -- one refusal now names the file and the four variables it found empty, the other names the character window it searched and its size, so a zero-length window can no longer read as an absent row.

rule_name: a declared upstream mirror is pinned by a test that reads upstream
pattern: A module states in prose that it re-implements a computation from an upstream tool -- the variable names verbatim, the numbered steps in the same order. Our half of the shared invariant is pinned by a test. The upstream half is not, so the sentence 'upstream does it this way' is true when it is typed and unchecked from then on. The re-implementation then drifts on a quantity the two sides read differently, the drift produces a wrong number rather than an error, and it surfaces later as an unrelated refusal in a different subsystem. A test on our side alone does not catch it: our side was already pinned when the drift happened, and it was pinned to the wrong value.
docstring: A borrowing stated only in prose is not a borrowing that is maintained. A module that mirrors an upstream computation must declare that machine-readably -- the upstream artefact, what is mirrored, and the test that pins it -- and the named test must exist, must define the named function, and must actually read the upstream artefact. A pin that asserts only our own invariant is the state this rule exists to improve on. Zero declared mirrors is NOT CHECKED and never PASS: a question with no subject is not a clean answer to it.
fix_action: Read (never import) each module's literal declaration; require the three fields, resolve the named pin file, require the named test to be defined in it, and require the pin to reference either the declared artefact path, its tail, or the declaration itself. Accept the third form deliberately: a pin that takes the path FROM the declaration keeps one copy of the fact, so the two cannot drift apart the way the mirror did -- and that form is what the gate's own first pin used, which is how the case was found. COUNT, and print on every run, the modules whose own prose claims a borrowing while declaring none; do not fail on them, because deciding whether a citation is a borrowing or a reference is a judgement this program has no input for, and turning a prose scan into a blocking predicate is how a checker earns a reputation for firing on correct code. MEASURED across three states: green against the real upstream artefact in the shipped image, RED against an upstream mutated to accumulate the other dimension, and an honest named skip on a host that ships no upstream at all. The pin also refuted the sentence the mirror had been documented with -- upstream does read the other dimension, twice, inside the same loop, and prints it without ever using it in arithmetic -- so the conclusion held and the stated evidence did not.

title: Two side-selecting option families use opposite axis vocabularies across one call boundary
problem: The pad module's IO-row command takes a horizontal and a vertical family of options (a site and a rotation in each) and applies the horizontal family to the EAST and WEST rows and the vertical family to the SOUTH and NORTH rows -- naming a row by the axis PERPENDICULAR to its run. The flow script that drives it names rows by the axis they RUN ALONG, in the same file that passes the options through, so each option family is delivered to the side-pair opposite the one the caller's own vocabulary assigns it. Nothing on either side of the boundary declares which convention is in force, and no error is raised.
golden_sample: none -- there is no expected-output artefact for this; the evidence is a pair of complementary sweeps and a geometry check, all reproducible from `docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-sha256-recovery/evidence/` (`probe_row.tcl`, `probe_row2.tcl`, `probe_site.tcl`, `probe_bbox.tcl`)
tool_enhancement: In the pad module's IO-row command, state which side-pair each option family governs -- in the command's own help text and in one informational line at call time naming the rows it just built and the option each took its orientation from. Better, accept unambiguous per-side aliases so a caller never has to know the convention. The driving flow script must then map its own side vocabulary onto the tool's explicitly rather than passing names through as if the two agreed. Verification: hold one family constant and sweep the other, then swap; the row orientations that move must be the ones the caller's documentation says that family controls.
pattern: Two layers of one shipped toolchain use the same axis words for opposite pairs of sides, and a configuration variable crosses over silently at the boundary between them. An author who sets the knob gets a real effect on the sides they did not name, and every single-axis experiment confirms 'this knob does nothing' -- because the sweep reads the sides that the OTHER knob steers while holding that other knob constant. The wrong conclusion is reproducible, survives being re-run in separate processes to remove a caching confound, and is refuted only by sweeping the complementary axis.
suggested_fix: Disclose the side-pair each option family governs at the tool's own interface, and reconcile the two vocabularies in the adapter that spans them.
session_context: Found while converging on a prior lane's conclusion that the vertical-rotation variable is inert. Four separate tool processes had shown the east/west orientation constant across every value of it. Sweeping the horizontal family instead moved east/west and left south/north still; a single call with two distinguishable sites and two different rotations then showed both families routing the same way, and the row bounding boxes confirmed the row names mean what they say. The data behind the inertness conclusion was correct; the conclusion was not.

title: A shipped refusal states a reason a later measurement contradicts
why_not_bucket_a: A program can detect the unsupported claim mechanically -- an inertness record that names one member of a variable family, whose siblings share its prefix in the module's own declared variable list, and whose stated evidence never mentions them. What a program cannot decide from that input is WHICH of two defensible behaviours the flow wants once the premise is corrected: keep the refusal and restate its reason, or drop it because the knob is live. That is a ruling about a shipped verdict, it was escalated once and ruled on the premise now refuted, and taking it unilaterally inside a capture brief is the scope creep the brief's own rules forbid.
pattern: A step refuses with a stated reason that was measured, published, ruled on, and built into shipped behaviour -- and the measurement behind it covered one axis of a multi-axis family. The refusal may still be the right behaviour, but the reason printed beside it is the part a reader acts on, and it is false. Correcting the reason and keeping the behaviour, or dropping the behaviour, are different decisions with different consequences, and the record cannot be left saying something the tree can be measured to contradict.
suggested_fix: Re-read the inertness record against the complementary-axis measurement, decide whether the refusal survives on the corrected premise, and restate the reason to match whichever way the decision goes. Then, separately, require that any future inertness claim name a sweep over every sibling of its variable family -- the siblings are derivable from the shared prefix in the module's own declared variable list, so the requirement is checkable.
session_context: The refusal and its inertness record are landed. The complementary-axis sweep that refutes the stated reason is in ``docs/capture/2026-08-22-jcapsha-sha256-recovery/evidence/`rotation_axis_vocabulary.md`, with the four scripts that reproduce it.

design: no design — found by reading the toolchain while writing an upstream pin
title: One step's two code paths pass the die rectangle's coordinates in opposite order
problem: A seal-ring step dispatches on PDK name into two branches that invoke the same generator. The die rectangle is declared as four corner coordinates, so one index is an x and the other a y. The generic branch passes them as width and height in that order; the other branch passes them in the opposite order. The receiving generator's own docstring states which axis each of its two parameters is, so this is not a naming ambiguity — one branch is simply wrong. Both values are valid numbers in valid units, nothing downstream re-derives the ring's extents from the die, and the generator's own usage example is a square die, so the defect is invisible except on a rectangular one.
golden_sample: the correct branch in the same file and the receiving script's own parameter documentation, both quoted in the bad_sample record
tool_enhancement: Make the two branches pass the die rectangle through ONE helper that derives the extents once from the declared corner order, so neither branch can pass a coordinate as an extent or transpose the two. Then refuse, rather than silently generate, when an extent arrives non-positive. Verification: drive both branches on a deliberately RECTANGULAR die and require the generated ring's bounding box to match the die's own aspect ratio in both — a square fixture cannot see this and is the reason it survived.
pattern: One step has two code paths to the same external tool, selected by a name rather than by a capability. The paths pass a two-component quantity — a width and a height, a row and a column, a min and a max — and one of them transposes the pair. Every fixture is symmetric in that quantity, so both paths agree on every test, and the error appears only on asymmetric real input, where it produces a plausible wrong artefact instead of an error. A pin written against the tool finds it; nothing that exercises only one path ever can.
suggested_fix: Derive the extents once, in one helper both paths call, and refuse a non-positive extent instead of generating from it.
session_context: Found while writing the upstream PIN required by this lane's mirror rule, not by running anything. Reading the contract in order to assert it is what surfaced the disagreement between the two branches; the pin itself is deliberately scoped to the branch this repo drives, so it neither blesses the transposition nor reddens over a defect in a path it does not use.
